title: Use a small ritual to connect remembrance with action

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: A ritual can organize attention through a repeated symbolic form. Its meaning, actual enactment and any promised later action are separate. A missed action does not prove the participant’s inner sincerity was false, but it remains missed.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Original fictional closing ritual: Jo places an owned smooth stone on the desk, names a friend’s welcome help, acknowledges an overdue borrowed card, chooses to return it Thursday 16:00 and begins 10 minutes of rest. The friend is not present; no sacred tradition is claimed. The desk accepts returns at that time.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Identify each element’s function and what would count as performed ritual versus completed repair. Choose an accessible private version without requiring disclosure.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A participant uses silent written recollection and declines sharing a loss. Does that make the ritual invalid?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Object, acknowledgment, unresolved matter, next action and rest have distinct roles. Later fiction: the ritual and rest occur, but Thursday’s return is missed. Preserve both; revise the return arrangement without calling the ritual a completed repair or diagnosing empty faith. Partial: report only the meaningful feeling. Incorrect: say speaking the intention returned the card.
criteria: Symbolic act and later conduct differ
Privacy and optional participation remain real
A missed action is retained without judging inner worth

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. An agreed accessible/private form can preserve remembrance and intention. Do not require grief disclosure or an emotional display as proof of meaning.
